first.rationale: Onboarding completion is down 4% QoQ and activation is down 6% QoQ. Memory 86 and 31 both demonstrate that simplifying onboarding (reducing friction, cutting required fields) produces durable lifts in completion and early activation. These are directly addressing the current performance decline. Memory 91 suggests activation messaging compounds the effect. While promotional pricing (memory_73) addresses competitive pressure, it risks margin and trains price-sensitive behavior. Enterprise sales assist (memory_44) is too narrow for the breadth of the problem. Referral incentives (memory_57) depend on retention health we haven't verified is stable. Verifying memory_86 and memory_31 will confirm whether a streamlined signup/onboarding intervention can restore the 4-6% lost ground. A standard_experiment scope allows rollout if validated, with capacity to adjust if results are unfavorable.

final.rationale: Archive records confirm both memories. Exp_86 shows +13% completion, -2.1 day time-to-value, +3% retention. Exp_31 shows +15% signup, +9% activation, +4% qualified revenue on SMB with only -1% retention risk. Current state shows onboarding completion down 4% and activation down 6% QoQ—directionally inverse to these proven interventions. Rerunning simplified onboarding as a standard_experiment addresses both current performance gaps with high-confidence precedent. The -1% retention risk in exp_31 is acceptable given the +9% activation and +4% qualified revenue lift, and the +3% retention gain in exp_86 partially offsets. SMB segment constraint from exp_31 is noted but the current crisis spans SMB price-sensitive accounts most acutely. This preserves long-term qualified revenue focus by restoring conversion efficiency rather than competing on margin via promotional pricing. Enterprise and referral levers remain available for future iterations.
